title: Chemical burn on the skin (acid, alkali, household cleaner)
summary: Acids, alkalis, bleach, lime, cement, and strong cleaning products keep damaging skin until they are washed away completely. Fast, long rinsing is the priority.
steps: Protect yourself — wear gloves or use a cloth so the chemical does not transfer to you.
Carefully remove any contaminated clothing or jewellery without dragging it over the face.
If the chemical is a dry powder (like lime or cement), brush it off the skin before rinsing.
Rinse the affected area with cool running water for at least 20 minutes — longer for strong acids or alkalis.
Keep the water running off the body so the chemical is not pushed onto unaffected skin.
Cover the area loosely with cling film (plastic wrap) or a clean, non-fluffy cloth after rinsing.
Note the name of the chemical and how long the person was exposed — tell the medics.
avoid: Do not try to neutralise the chemical with another substance (no vinegar on alkali, no baking soda on acid) — this can make the burn worse.
Do not apply oils, ointments, butter, or pastes.
Do not burst blisters or rub the skin.
Do not stop rinsing early because the pain has eased.
whenToEscalate: Always — chemical burns need medical assessment. Get to an emergency department after starting rinsing.
Immediately if the chemical reached the eyes, mouth, throat, or was inhaled.
Immediately if the burn is on the face, hands, feet, genitals, joints, or covers a large area.
If the person feels dizzy, short of breath, or unwell — this may indicate systemic exposure.
